kurz: Why few estates owe federal estate tax, how the annual gift exclusion and the step-up in basis work, and why beneficiary designations decide how fast heirs can get at an account.

bloecke.md:
Every brokerage account changes owner at the latest when its holder dies. Unlike the market, this change can be planned decades in advance. Two federal taxes are involved. The estate and gift tax applies to the transfer of wealth and is paid by the estate or the giver, not by the heir. The income tax applies to gains in the account, and here inheritance brings a large advantage: the heir's basis is generally reset to the value on the date of death, the **step-up in basis** (26 U.S.C. § 1014). Gains that built up during the deceased's lifetime are never taxed.

The value on the date of death is decisive for both. If the market falls after the death, the executor can elect an alternate valuation date six months later (§ 2032), but only if this reduces both the value of the gross estate and the estate tax. For estates that owe no estate tax, the election is therefore not available.

## Exemption, annual exclusion and rates

bloecke.md:
For federal purposes, the relationship between giver and recipient hardly matters. A child, a friend and an unmarried partner are treated alike; only a spouse who is a US citizen and charities receive transfers tax-free without limit. Transfers to grandchildren can also trigger the generation-skipping transfer tax, which has its own exemption of the same amount. For a spouse who is not a US citizen, the unlimited marital deduction does not apply; a higher annual exclusion and special trusts take its place.

State taxes are a different matter. About a dozen states and the District of Columbia levy their own estate tax, often with an exemption far below the federal one, Oregon for example from $1 million and Massachusetts from $2 million. A few states levy an inheritance tax on the recipient, and there the relationship does matter. In Pennsylvania, for example, transfers to a spouse are taxed at 0%, to children and grandchildren at 4.5%, to siblings at 12% and to all others at 15%. Where the deceased lived, and where real estate is located, therefore matters.

bloecke.md:
## Valuation of a portfolio at death

Listed stocks and ETFs are valued at the mean between the highest and lowest quoted selling prices on the valuation date (Treas. Reg. § 20.2031-2). Mutual fund shares are valued at their redemption price, the net asset value (§ 20.2031-8). Bank balances count at face value plus accrued interest. Real estate is valued at fair market value, usually by an appraisal.

The same values determine the heirs' basis, also for estates far below the exemption. Two groups of assets do not get a step-up. Retirement accounts such as traditional IRAs and 401(k)s are income in respect of a decedent: the heirs pay income tax on withdrawals as the deceased would have. And assets given away during life keep the giver's basis.

The father is widowed, and his daughter is the sole heir. On the date of death, the estate consists of a brokerage account worth $620,000, for which he paid $300,000 over the years, bank balances of $40,000 and a rented condo worth $400,000, bought for $250,000 and depreciated by $60,000.

- The gross estate is $1,060,000, far below the $15,000,000 exemption. No federal estate tax is due, and no federal estate tax return has to be filed.
- The daughter's basis in the portfolio is $620,000. If she sells right away, her gain is zero. The $320,000 of gains that accrued during her father's life are never taxed.
- Her basis in the condo is $400,000. The $210,000 of gain, including $60,000 of depreciation, on which her father would have owed tax in a sale, disappears as well.

Had the father sold the portfolio a month before his death, the $320,000 gain would have been taxable. If he lived in Pennsylvania, the state inheritance tax for a child of 4.5% applies, roughly $47,700 on $1,060,000 before deductions for debts and expenses. Holding appreciated assets until death is one of the most effective income tax strategies in the US. Assets with a loss, by contrast, get a step-down, so their losses can only be used if they are realized during life.

bloecke.titel: The annual exclusion renews every year
bloecke.md: Gifts up to the annual exclusion of $19,000 per recipient (2026) are tax-free and use up nothing. The amount applies per giver and per recipient and renews on January 1 every year. A married couple can give $38,000 a year to each child, and the child's spouse and each grandchild can receive the same. For a 529 college savings plan, five years of exclusions can be front-loaded in one year, $95,000 per giver and beneficiary. Gifts above the exclusion require Form 709, due April 15 of the following year, but they only reduce the lifetime exemption; tax arises only when lifetime gifts and the estate together exceed it. Of all the planning options, this is the only one that costs nothing but time.

bloecke.md:
The table shows the central trade-off. A gift moves future growth out of the estate, but the recipient takes over the giver's basis (§ 1015); if the value at the time of the gift is below the giver's basis, a later loss is limited to the lower value. A bequest saves the income tax on all gains accrued until death. With a federal exemption of $15 million, the income tax effect matters far more for most families than estate tax. Giving away highly appreciated shares during life is therefore usually the more expensive route, unless the estate is large enough to owe estate tax.

## Trusts and life estates

A **revocable living trust** holds assets during the owner's life and passes them to the beneficiaries at death without probate. For tax purposes, it changes nothing: the assets remain part of the estate and receive the step-up. An **irrevocable trust** can remove assets and their future growth from the estate, but assets given to it during life generally keep the giver's basis. A life estate, in which the owner keeps the right to use or live in a property for life and the remainder passes to a child, keeps the property in the owner's estate and therefore preserves the step-up (§ 2036).

bloecke.md: The unused exclusion of the first spouse to die (DSUE) only passes to the survivor if the executor files a complete estate tax return, Form 706, and elects portability, even when no tax is due. If the estate does not otherwise have to file, a simplified late election is available for up to five years after the death (Rev. Proc. 2022-32). Without it, the first spouse's unused exclusion of up to $15 million is lost. For couples whose combined wealth, including future growth, could exceed one exemption, this filing is cheap insurance.

## The home

Inherited real estate also receives a step-up. In the community property states, such as California, Texas and Arizona, both halves of community property receive a new basis at the first spouse's death (§ 1014(b)(6)); in other states, only the deceased spouse's half of jointly owned property does. A surviving spouse who has not remarried and sells the main home within two years after the death can still use the $500,000 exclusion for married couples (§ 121(b)(4)), provided the requirements were met before the death. Since the step-up already removes most of the gain, the exclusion often only has to cover the increase in value after the death.

Traditional IRAs and 401(k)s receive no step-up. Most beneficiaries other than a spouse must empty an inherited account within ten years under the SECURE Act of 2019, and if the owner had already started required distributions, annual distributions are also required in the meantime. Every withdrawal from a traditional account is ordinary income for the heir, often in their highest-earning years. Inherited Roth IRAs are subject to the same ten-year rule, but the withdrawals are tax-free.

The beneficiary named on the account decides who receives it, not the will. A designation that was never updated after a divorce or a death leads to the wrong person receiving the account. For employer plans governed by federal law, the Supreme Court held that the designation on file prevails even over state laws that revoke designations upon divorce (Egelhoff v. Egelhoff, 2001).

## Access to the account

When a broker learns of the death, it freezes the account until someone proves the right to act. How long this takes depends on how the account is titled. Accounts with a **transfer on death (TOD)** registration, bank accounts with a payable on death (POD) designation, retirement accounts with a named beneficiary and joint accounts with right of survivorship pass directly to the named person on presentation of a death certificate and the institution's forms, often within weeks. Everything else goes through **probate**: a court appoints an executor or administrator, who receives letters testamentary or letters of administration, opens an estate account with its own taxpayer identification number and distributes the assets. Depending on the state and the estate, probate takes months to more than a year and costs court and attorney fees. Most states offer a simplified procedure or a small estate affidavit below a threshold set by state law.

A power of attorney ends at death. A durable power of attorney is nevertheless indispensable for the case of incapacity during life; without it, a court has to appoint a guardian or conservator, even for a spouse. After the death, only the executor, the successor trustee of a living trust or the named beneficiary can act.

When there are several heirs, the executor administers the estate on their behalf. Securities are usually distributed in kind into the heirs' own accounts. This is not a sale and as a rule does not trigger income tax; each heir takes over the stepped-up basis.

bloecke.md: The executor files the deceased's final Form 1040 for the year of death, covering income up to the date of death. Capital loss carryovers of the deceased can only be used on this final return and are lost afterward. Income the estate receives later, such as dividends before the account is distributed, is reported on Form 1041 if it reaches $600. Form 706 is required if the gross estate plus adjusted taxable gifts exceeds the basic exclusion amount, and otherwise only to elect portability. Gifts above the annual exclusion are reported by the giver on Form 709 by April 15 of the following year. Banks and brokers do not report an estate to the IRS for estate tax purposes; each of these filings is the responsibility of the executor or the giver.

Name primary and contingent beneficiaries on every IRA, 401(k) and life insurance policy, and add a TOD or POD designation to brokerage and bank accounts. Review them after every marriage, divorce, birth and death.

A will must meet the formal requirements of your state, usually signing before witnesses. A revocable living trust avoids probate for the assets transferred into it, but only if they are actually retitled to the trust.

A list of all accounts, policies, property and digital access, kept separately from the passwords and checked every year. Without such a list, heirs spend months searching, and forgotten accounts end up with the state as unclaimed property.

bloecke.titel: Spousal rights and the limits of disinheritance
bloecke.md: In most US states, children can be disinherited entirely; there is no forced share for children, with the exception of Louisiana, which protects children under 24 and children who are permanently unable to care for themselves. Spouses, by contrast, are protected. In the community property states, each spouse already owns half of the community property. In most other states, a surviving spouse can claim an elective share of the estate instead of what the will provides, often around one third, with rules that vary by state. Some states include assets that pass outside probate, such as accounts with a TOD designation or recent gifts, in the calculation. A plan that is optimal for tax purposes can therefore fail if a spouse's statutory rights are ignored.
